claims.text: Replacing full ab initio thermodynamic integration with machine-learned-potential two-phase coexistence simulations can yield melting properties for refractory materials.
The resulting melting properties will be comparably accurate to DFT-based predictions.
The proposed method will cost substantially less than full ab initio thermodynamic integration.
NbMoTaW is an example of a single-phase, high-melting refractory high-entropy alloy.
The target refractory material has complex electronic and atomic disorder.
A machine-learned interatomic potential can be developed from a limited set of DFT training data.
Two-phase coexistence molecular dynamics can replace full ab initio thermodynamic integration for the proposed calculation.
A sufficiently large simulation cell can accommodate coexisting solid and liquid phases.
A microcanonical simulation can be used to monitor phase fluctuations near the melting point.
The solid-liquid interface mediates atomic rearrangements between the two phases.
The solid-liquid interface mediates the free-energy relationship between the solid and liquid phases.
An adequately trained machine-learned potential reproduces key DFT energetic features of the material.
An adequately trained machine-learned potential reproduces key DFT structural features of the material.
A two-phase coexistence simulation naturally equilibrates at the melting temperature.
The melting temperature can be estimated directly from energy and density behavior in the coexistence simulation.
Entropy and enthalpy of fusion can be obtained from discontinuities associated with the solid-liquid transition.
The volume change at melting can be obtained from the solid-liquid density difference.
The predicted melting properties will deviate by approximately 5–10% from high-fidelity DFT predictions and experimental observations.
The computational savings will be sufficient to enable high-throughput screening of refractory materials.
Accuracy may degrade for systems with very complex bonding or scarce and insufficiently diverse DFT training data.
